verdict.rationale: LangGraph ships interrupts as a first-party feature. They pause graph execution at specific points and wait for external input, and the graph resumes via Command, backed by checkpointer persistence for human-in-the-loop workflows and compile-time breakpoints. That gives a native way to gate a node, such as a sensitive tool step, on human input. The evidence never explicitly documents approving or rejecting individual tool calls, so the per-tool approval policy has to be wired by the developer. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of per-tool-call approval gating (approve/edit/reject of specific tool invocations), a worked example of interrupting before a sensitive tool executes, and independent hands-on corroboration of approval gating.

support.subject: As an engineering-lead, I can require human approval before specific sensitive tool calls execute

citations.quote: Interrupts allow you to pause graph execution at specific points and wait for external input before continuing.
you resume execution by re-invoking the graph using Command, which then becomes the return value of the interrupt() call from inside the node
It is also where you can specify runtime args like checkpointers and breakpoints.
Human-in-the-loop — Seamlessly incorporate human oversight by inspecting and modifying agent state at any point during execution.
